# 2 Samuel 6 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter records David's two attempts to bring the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem: the first ending in tragedy (Uzzah's death), the second in triumph. Ellicott notes that 1 Chronicles 13–16 gives a much fuller parallel account, and suggests Psalms 68, 24, 101, 15, and 132 are associated with these events. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)

Youngblood (Expositor's Bible Commentary) outlines it as a chiasm: A – Unsuccessful attempt (vv.1–5); B – Judgment on Uzzah (vv.6–11); A′ – Successful attempt (vv.12–19); B′ – Judgment on Michal (vv.20–23). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-6-commentary)

---

## v.1 — David again assembled the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand in all.

- **Ellicott**: "Again" should be read with "gathered together" — referring to former military musters. The 30,000 represented "all Israel" (1 Chr 13:5). The LXX reads 70,000. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: David gathered so many soldiers because bringing the ark to Jerusalem was an "important step towards providing a central place of worship for all of Israel." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Precept Austin**: Notes that David consulted with captains and leaders (1 Chr 13:1-4) but failed to consult the LORD. "The majority opinion is not always correct! Only God's opinion matters!" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-6-commentary)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The time had come for the ark's restoration as the centre of national worship. The union of the tribes under David, conquest of Jerusalem, and defeat of the Philistines prepared the way. David was impelled by "a truly theocratic spirit." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_samuel/6.htm)

---

## v.2 — He and all his troops set out for Baale of Judah to bring up the ark of God…the name of the LORD of Hosts, who is enthroned between the cherubim.

- **Ellicott**: Baale is another name for Kirjath-jearim (Josh 15:9; 1 Chr 13:6), where the ark had been since its return from the Philistines. "Whose name is called" — the ark is the visible symbol of God's presence and covenant. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: The ark represented "the immediate presence and glory of God in Israel." It had sat at Abinadab's house for 20+ years. David wanted Israel "alive with a sense of the near presence and glory of God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Precept Austin**: The ark is "called by the Name" — an idiom of ownership, emphasizing it is the Lord's property. "The Name" also stands for His presence (cf. Deut 12:5, 11). The ark had languished an estimated 50–70 years. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-6-commentary)
- **J. Vernon McGee** (cited at Precept Austin): David "did not have some peculiar superstition about the ark. He knew where the Lord was…but he knew that the approach to God was made through the ark which spoke of a mediator between God and man." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-6-commentary)
- **Gill**: "Whose name is called by the name of the Lord of hosts" — not the ark, but the Lord whose the ark is; the ark belonged to Him who dwells between the cherubim. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/6.htm)

---

## v.3 — They set the ark of God on a new cart…Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were guiding the new cart.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Transporting the ark on a cart violated God's command. The ark was designed to be carried (Ex 25:12-15) only by Kohathite Levites (Num 4:15). "God wanted the ark to be carried because He wanted nothing mechanical about the ark representing His presence" (quoting Alan Redpath). The Philistines used a cart (1 Sam 6:10-11) and "got away with it because they were Philistines, but God expected more from His people." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: The new cart "was doubtless intended as a mark of respect (comp. 1 Sam 6:7); yet it was a violation of the law (Num 7:9)." He adds charitably: "the ark having been left neglected for more than two generations, the exact requirements in regard to it may easily have passed out of mind." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)
- **Benson**: Notes that no wagons were allowed to the Kohathites; they were to carry the ark on their shoulders (Num 7:9). "It is matter of astonishment…how David and all the priests and people could fall into so great" an error. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/2-samuel-6.html)
- **Precept Austin**: "It worked for the Philistines so it should be good enough for us!" — warns against imitating worldly methods. The poles were still in the rings, making the cart doubly inexcusable. Uzzah means "strength" and Ahio means "friendly" — "much service for the LORD is like this — a new cart, a big production, with strength leading and a friendly image presented out front — yet all done without inquiring of God." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-6-commentary)
- **Constable**: David moved the ark "according to customary practice (cf. 1 Samuel 6:7-8)" rather than Mosaic Law. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-6.html)

---

## v.4 — Bringing with it the ark of God. And Ahio was walking in front of the ark.

- **Ellicott**: The text has "undoubtedly suffered" through scribal repetition. The whole verse is omitted in the parallel in 1 Chronicles 13, and the first half (a repetition of v.3) is omitted in the LXX. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)

---

## v.5 — David and all the house of Israel were celebrating before the LORD with all kinds of wood instruments, harps, stringed instruments, tambourines, sistrums, and cymbals.

- **Ellicott**: "Played" means dancing accompanied by music (cf. 1 Sam 18:7). "On all manner of instruments made of fir wood" — the parallel in 1 Chr 13:8 has "with all their might and with songs." The Hebrew difference is slight; Chronicles is likely the correct reading. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: This was "quite a production" — joyful and exciting — "The problem was that none of it pleased God because it was all in disobedience to His word." Warns against judging worship by how it makes us feel rather than whether it pleases God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Alarm Redpath** (cited at Enduring Word): "We want God's presence very much, don't we? But we like to hitch His presence to some of our new carts…How much of our service is really in the energy of the flesh?" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)

---

## vv.6-7 — When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reached out…God struck him down on the spot for his irreverence, and he died there beside the ark of God.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Uzzah's touching the ark violated Num 4:15 — "they shall not touch any holy thing, lest they die." God "fulfilled the ominous promise." Uzzah's error was a "critical error in thinking": (1) it didn't matter who carried the ark; (2) it didn't matter how; (3) he knew all about it because it was in his father's house; (4) God couldn't take care of the ark Himself; (5) the ground was less holy than his hand. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Maclaren** (cited at Enduring Word): "He saw no difference between the ark and any other valuable article. His intention to help was right enough; but there was a profound insensibility to the awful sacredness of the ark." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: Uzzah was probably a Levite and "ought to have made himself familiar with the law." What may seem severe was "a very necessary manifestation of the Divine displeasure," involving "not only a violation of the letter of the law…but a want of reverence for the majesty of God as symbolised by the ark." Quotes O. von Gerlach: "Uzzah was a type of all who, with good intentions…yet with unsanctified minds, interfere in the affairs of the kingdom of God, from the notion that they are in danger, and with the hope of saving them." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)
- **Benson (Methodist)**: Uzzah's error was (1) not carrying the ark on his shoulders with his brethren, (2) touching it, which Levites too were forbidden from doing under penalty of death (Num 4:15-20). Also, Uzzah's action showed "want of faith, in the presence of God with the ark, and in his power, as if he were not able to preserve that sacred symbol of his presence from falling." Adds from Poole: "God's smiting Uzzah…may seem very severe, considering his intention was pious…But…it is reasonable God should make some present examples of his high displeasure against sins seemingly small…for the establishment of discipline, and for the greater terror and caution of mankind." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/2-samuel-6.html)
- **Ligonier (Reformed)**: "Uzzah likely had a good intent…But the fact that he transported the ark wrongly and did not obey the Lord's warning not to touch the ark showed just how far his heart was from true obedience…Because of sin, his hands were dirtier than the ground the ark was in danger of touching." Adds: "What should surprise us is not that the Lord sometimes executes His wrath immediately but that He does not do so more often." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/uzzahs-error)
- **Constable**: The death of Uzzah parallels Nadab and Abihu (Lev 10:1-2), Achan (Josh 7), and Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1-11) — all failed to take God seriously "at the beginning of a new phase of His kingdom program." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-6.html)
- **Gaebelein**: David neglected divine instructions; "the way they transported the ark was the way of the Philistines (1 Samuel 6:7)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-samuel-6.html)

---

## vv.8-9 — Then David became angry…he named that place Perez-uzzah…David feared the LORD and asked, "How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?"

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: David's anger was "based upon confusion. He couldn't understand why his good intentions weren't enough. God cares about both our intentions and actions." His question "How can the ark come to me?" was answered later by returning to God's word — "To the law and to the testimony!" (Isa 8:20). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: "Was displeased" = "was angry." His vexation was at the Divine judgment upon Uzzah, but "it does not follow that he was angry with God, but rather was simply vexed and disturbed at this most untoward interruption of his plans." Perez-uzzah = "breach of Uzzah" (same word as Ex 19:22). The fear was "that awe of the majesty of God in which they had shown themselves deficient. If this was at first excessive, it was soon moderated." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)
- **Ligonier (Reformed)**: David "confused good intentions with obedience," and the chapter shows him learning the lesson. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blessing-and-curse-of-the-ark)

---

## vv.10-11 — He was unwilling to move the ark…took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite…the LORD blessed him and all his household.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "David did this in fulfillment of God's word." Obed-edom was a Levite of the family of Korah and Kohath (1 Chr 26:4) — the very family commanded to carry the ark (Num 4:15). "When God's word was obeyed, and His holiness was respected, blessing followed." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: Obed-edom was a Levite (either Kohathite or Merarite). "Gittite" means born at or belonging to Gath-rimmon, a Levitical city (Josh 21:24-25). The Obed-edom of 1 Chr 26:4-5 is noted as one "God blessed," likely referring to this passage. He later became a porter, musician, and minister before the ark. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)
- **Ligonier (Reformed)**: "The actual presence of the ark was a source of blessing for an obedient people, as seen in the blessings that came to the house of Obed-edom." God's curse was not inevitable where the ark was — obedience made the difference. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blessing-and-curse-of-the-ark)

---

## v.12 — Now it was reported to King David, "The LORD has blessed the house of Obed-edom…because of the ark of God." So David went and had the ark…brought up…with rejoicing.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "David was glad to know that the presence and glory of God could bring blessing instead of a curse. He was also glad to see that when they obeyed God they were blessed." David later explained to the priests: "because you did not do it the first time, the LORD our God broke out against us, because we did not consult Him about the proper order" (1 Chr 15:13). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: David's immediate reason was the blessings on Obed-edom, "yet this implies neither jealousy nor a wish to deprive his subject of a blessing. It had been his original purpose…he had only desisted in a fit of vexation and then of fear. He now saw that such fear was groundless." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)
- **Ligonier (Reformed)**: "David learned an important lesson about following the Lord's regulations for worship." He told the people only Levites could transport the ark, and the Levites "returned to their sacred role." The tent David built in Jerusalem was "not the tabernacle" — the tabernacle and altar remained at Gibeon (1 Chr 16:39-40). (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ark-comes-to-jerusalem)

---

## v.13 — When those carrying the ark of the LORD had advanced six paces, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "Those bearing the ark" — David now had Levites carrying it on their shoulders (1 Chr 15:11-15). The sacrifice after six paces was "elaborate, excessive, over-the-top sacrifice…communicated atonement, consecration, and longing for fellowship." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: "David no longer presumed to violate the law, but took care that the ark should be borne by the proper persons." In 1 Chronicles 15 a detailed account is given of the sanctification of priests and Levites. "It is quite unnecessary to suppose that offerings were made at each six steps of the way…The work was begun and ended with solemn sacrifice." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)

---

## vv.14-15 — David, wearing a linen ephod, danced with all his might before the LORD, while he and all the house of Israel brought up the ark…with shouting and the sounding of the ram's horn.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "David didn't hold back anything in his own expression of worship. He didn't dance out of obligation but out of heartfelt worship." The linen ephod was not immodest — 1 Chr 15:27 shows David was dressed just like the priests and Levites. "He set aside his royal robes and dressed just like everyone else in the procession." The dancing was "appropriate in the context" — a parade/marching band procession, not a solo performance, but "simple rhythmic steps together with other men in the way one might see Orthodox Jewish men today dance." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: "The religious dances on occasions of great national blessing were usually performed by women only (Ex 15:20-21; Jdg 11:34; 1 Sam 18:6). The king, by now taking part in them himself, marked his strong sense of the importance of the occasion, and his readiness to do his utmost in God's honour." On the ephod: the linen ephod (bad) was not the high priest's ephod (shesh); it was "simply a garment worn by any one engaged in a religious service," also worn by Samuel (1 Sam 2:18). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)
- **Ligonier (Reformed)**: "David even helped lead in the worship, wearing the same kind of fine linen that the Levites wore and offering sacrifices…Ordinarily, the king did not lead in worship in that manner, but this was a special occasion, and David was a special king. In his actions here, we have a type of the King to come who would be both Priest and King, the Lord Jesus Christ." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ark-comes-to-jerusalem)

---

## v.16 — As the ark of the LORD was entering the City of David, Saul's daughter Michal looked down from a window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Michal "didn't appreciate David's exuberant worship. She felt it wasn't dignified for the king of Israel to express his emotions before God." Quotes Spurgeon: "No doubt, there are particularly nice and dainty people who will censure God's chosen if they live wholly to his praise, and they will call them eccentric, old-fashioned, obstinate, absurd…From the window of their superiority they look down upon us." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: "The contrast is here strongly brought out between the spirit of Saul's house in which Michal had been brought up, and that of David. In Saul's time the ark had been neglected, and true religion was uncared for. Michal, therefore, who had fallen in love with David as a brave hero, could not understand the religious enthusiasm which led him to rank himself among the common people before the Lord." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)

---

## vv.17-19 — They brought the ark…set it in its place inside the tent that David had pitched…David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings…blessed the people in the name of the LORD of Hosts…distributed to every man and woman…a loaf of bread, a date cake, and a raisin cake.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: The ark was "set in the Most Holy Place." The burnt offerings spoke of consecration, the peace offerings of fellowship. The food distribution was a fellowship meal. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: The "tabernacle" was not the wilderness tabernacle (which was at Gibeon) but "a special tent which David…had prepared for it." David's blessing of the people was "eminently fitting" but "is by no means to be mistaken for the peculiar priestly blessing for which the form was prescribed in Num 6:22-26." On the food: "a good piece of flesh" — a unique word; "a flagon of wine" should be translated "a cluster of grapes or raisins" (cf. 1 Chr 16:3; Song 2:5; Hos 3:1). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)

---

## v.20 — As soon as David returned home to bless his own household, Saul's daughter Michal came out to meet him. "How the king of Israel has distinguished himself today!…He has uncovered himself…like a vulgar person would do."

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "With biting sarcasm, Michal's criticism could have ruined this whole day for David." She objected to what David wore, not just his dancing. "David acted as if he were just another worshipper in Israel." Quotes Spurgeon: "Pirates look out for loaded vessels" — the attack came after his greatest spiritual high. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: Michal saw David from the window as he passed by the house with the ark. Now, David returns "to bless those members of his household whom eastern custom had not allowed to take part in the ceremonies, and is met by Michal with her cutting irony." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)

---

## vv.21-22 — David said to Michal, "I was dancing before the LORD, who chose me over your father and all his house…I will celebrate before the LORD, and I will humiliate and humble myself even more than this."

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: David didn't let Michal ruin his day. "I did it for God, not for you." David "did not say, 'Over my people': he acknowledged that they were not his people, but Jehovah's people" (quoting Spurgeon). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: "David first gives the true and sufficient reason of his conduct—what he had done was before the Lord, in honouring whom no man can be really humbled; and then he turns with a reproof to Michal, which should have shown her the utter unworthiness of her objections. God had set aside her father and his house for this very spirit of pride in which she was now indulging, and had chosen him instead." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)
- **Spurgeon (Baptist/Reformed)**: Preached an entire sermon on these verses emphasizing divine election. "David justified what he had done by God's choice of him." He makes five points on the effect of knowing one's election: (1) It makes God the leading thought; (2) It creates a proper disregard for human opinion; (3) It causes a low opinion of self; (4) It stirs a desire for God's service; (5) It creates exultant joy. "The doctrines of grace put the very idea of honouring man out of court with us." (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/david-dancing-before-the-ark-because-of-his-election)

---

## v.23 — And Michal the daughter of Saul had no children to the day of her death.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Michal's barrenness "was not necessarily the result of Divine judgment. It may be that David never had marital relations with her again. Nevertheless, the principle stands: there is often barrenness in the life and ministry of the overly critical." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)
- **Ellicott**: "The severest privation to an Oriental woman. It is quite possible that during Michal's long separation from David, while he was an outlaw, and she was married to Phaltiel…they had become somewhat alienated from each other; and when the totally different spirit by which they were animated was brought out on this occasion, David determined to have no further intercourse with her." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/6.htm)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed / Ligonier
The Reformed reading strongly emphasises the **regulative principle of worship** — God must be worshipped only as He has commanded. Ligonier stresses that David's first attempt failed because "the people were not following what the law said regarding the transport of the ark" and notes the contrast between Uzzah's judgment and Obed-edom's blessing shows "the Lord takes His worship seriously." The ark's proper transport by Levites prefigures Christ as Priest-King. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ark-comes-to-jerusalem; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/uzzahs-error)

### Baptist / Spurgeon
Spurgeon reads the chapter through the lens of **divine election**. David's defence — "the LORD…chose me before thy father" — becomes the centrepiece. "The effect upon you of your knowing your election of God will be similar to the effect which it had upon David." He also emphasises that election produces bold disregard for human opinion in worship: "The man who says, 'God has chosen me,' can afford to let others think and speak after their own nature." Michal's criticism is met with David's reply rooted in sovereign grace, not human merit. (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/david-dancing-before-the-ark-because-of-his-election)

### Pentecostal/Charismatic / Enduring Word (David Guzik)
Guzik stresses both **obedience to God's Word** and the **freedom of emotional, heartfelt worship**. David dancing "with all his might" is celebrated as genuine, not manipulated. At the same time, the first attempt's failure is squarely on disobedience. The balance: "There are two great errors in this area — the error of making emotions the center of our Christian life and the error of an emotionally detached Christian life." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-6/)

### Methodist/Wesleyan
Adam Clarke (Methodist) and Joseph Benson (Methodist) emphasise Uzzah's **double error**: (1) not carrying the ark on shoulders, (2) touching it. Benson adds the lack-of-faith dimension — Uzzah acted "as if [God] were not able to preserve that sacred symbol." They also quote Poole's sober note that God's severity is actually merciful, establishing discipline. (Clarke's full commentary was not retrieved due to limits, but Benson's was partially accessed at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/2-samuel-6.html)

### Dispensational / Gaebelein
Gaebelein stresses that the ark transport method was "the way of the Philistines" and that "Godly fear and faithful submission to the Word of God are essentials in true service for God." He treats Chronicles as giving the theocratic perspective while Samuel provides the outward, historical view. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-samuel-6.html)

## What Could Not Be Found (within search/fetch limits)

- **Lutheran-specific** readings from LCMS or 1517.org — no results returned.
- **Catholic/Orthodox** readings from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org — no results returned.
- **Modern scholarly** readings from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org — no results returned.
- **Prosperity / Word of Faith / hyper-grace** readings — no results returned. (These traditions would typically emphasise the blessing on Obed-edom's house as a "principle" of ark-presence bringing material prosperity, but no specific site from the approved list addressed this.)
- **Methodist/Wesleyan** from wesley.nnu.edu or seedbed.com — not returned; Clarke/Benson (Methodist-leaning) were partially accessed through StudyLight.
